title: Why the Apple Doesn't Fall Far: Understanding Intergenerational Transmission of Human Capital
research_question: Does a parent's level of education causally affect the educational attainment of their children, or do observed positive correlations between parental and child education primarily reflect selection on family characteristics and inherited ability? Specifically, what is the spillover effect on the next generation of policies that raise parental schooling at the lower tail of the education distribution?
data_description: The analysis uses linked Norwegian administrative registers covering the entire population aged 16-74, merged with the 1960 Census (used to assign parents to the municipality where they grew up) and the 1970 Census (for older cohorts' education). The parent sample comprises cohorts born 1947-1958, while the child sample consists of their children aged 25-35 in 2000. Key variables include years of completed education (reported by educational institutions to Statistics Norway, minimizing measurement error), earnings, age, sex, and parent's childhood municipality. Reform timing for each municipality is taken primarily from Ness (1971) and verified against breaks in the share with fewer than 9 years of schooling; reform indicators are assigned for 545 of 728 municipalities (74% of the sample). Summary statistics cover roughly 173,000 children, 145,000 mothers, and 97,000 fathers.
institutional_context: In 1959, the Norwegian Parliament legislated a major compulsory schooling reform that raised mandatory education from 7 to 9 years, kept the school starting age at 7, standardized the curriculum, and expanded school access. Implementation was staggered across municipalities between 1960 and 1972, with municipalities required to submit plans to the Ministry of Education for approval and federal funding for teachers and buildings. The committee aimed for representative rollout, and prior research finds little association between municipality characteristics (income, education, age, urban status, industry mix, unemployment, Labor party share) and the timing of adoption. The first cohort potentially affected was born in 1947 and the last cohort that could remain under the old system was born in 1958. The reform substantially compressed the lower tail of the schooling distribution, reducing the share with fewer than 9 years of education from about 12% to 3%, and prior work documents positive earnings returns to the induced schooling.
